notes: Complex multi-party hazelnut receivables dispute; Brussels Regulation jurisdiction analysis and partial stays are clearly reasoned despite voluminous evidence.

enrichment.short_title: Hazelnut loan fraud: Brussels Regulation jurisdiction over bank and Ferrero claims

statutes_considered.title: Brussels Convention on jurisdiction and the enforcement of judgments in civil and commercial matters

key_facts: BTM and KBC lent about €22.8 million to Turkish hazelnut exporter Baskan Gida secured on receivables from the Ferrero group under a framework supply contract.
Baskan Gida allegedly forged Ferrero acknowledgements of assignment and drew down most of the facility without repaying the banks.
The banks sued Baskan Gida and related parties in England while Ferrero Italy and Ferrero Industrial commenced negative-declaration proceedings in Alba, Italy.
The banks also pursued tort, conversion, knowing receipt and tracing claims against Ferrero group companies.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application to strike out or stay English proceedings and for permission to amend, raising Brussels Convention jurisdiction and lis pendens issues.
enrichment.outcome: Contractual claims against Ferrero Italy and Ferrero Industrial stayed pending Italian jurisdictional rulings; contractual claims against Ferrero Germany and Ferrero France stayed under Article 28; tort claims may proceed in England with amendments allowed.
enrichment.ratio: Under the Brussels Convention, related contractual claims subject to pending Italian negative-declaration proceedings must be stayed under Articles 27 and 28 where the Italian court may have jurisdiction, but tortious and quasi-tortious claims raising no common issues with those contractual proceedings are not related actions and may continue in England.
legal_issues: Whether English proceedings should be stayed for lis pendens under Article 27
Whether Article 28 required a discretionary stay of related contractual claims
Whether tort, conversion and tracing claims were related actions to the Italian contractual proceedings
Whether the English court had jurisdiction under Articles 5 and 6 over the tort claims

notes: Trade mark opposition appeal preliminary application; section 12 construction under the 1938 Act and Ladd v Marshall refusal are clear.

enrichment.short_title: Goldfischli trade mark appeal: refusal of late section 12 case and fresh evidence
key_facts: Kambly opposed Intersnack's registration of Goldfischli device and word marks for goldfish-shaped crackers.
The assistant registrar rejected Kambly's opposition and Kambly appealed shortly before the hearing.
Kambly sought to amend grounds to rely on section 12 and to add eight witness statements about US base sales not raised before the registrar.
Intersnack had earlier succeeded in removing Kambly's marks from the register for five-year non-use.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Pre-appeal application for permission to amend grounds of opposition and appeal and to admit fresh evidence.
enrichment.outcome: Both applications dismissed; the section 12 point was rejected as bad in law and the fresh evidence was refused.
enrichment.ratio: Under the 1938 Act, section 12 bars registration only if an identical or similar mark remains on the register at the date of registration, not merely at the date of application; late new points and fresh evidence will rarely be allowed on trade mark appeals where the case could have been raised earlier and issue estoppel applies to prior non-user findings.
legal_issues: Whether section 12 barred registration because Kambly's marks were on the register when Intersnack applied
Whether Kambly should be permitted to raise a section 12 case for the first time on appeal
Whether fresh evidence of sales at US military bases should be admitted under Ladd v Marshall principles
Whether issue estoppel from the non-user rectification decision precluded reliance on the new evidence

notes: USS pension preservation issue; section 180 normal pension age analysis and OPB correspondence are clearly resolved.

enrichment.short_title: USS deferred benefits: individual normal pension age under section 180
key_facts: The Universities Superannuation Scheme trustee applied actuarial reductions when deferred members with contractual retirement below 65 took preserved benefits at age 60.
Members argued normal pension age under section 180 depended on each member's contract of employment, not a uniform scheme age of 65.
The trustee had administered the scheme on a uniform male normal pension age of 65 for many years with OPB correspondence in the 1990s.
Affected classes included male members with pre-1990 service and members with post-1995 service and contractual retirement below 63.5.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Part 8 claim for declarations on the proper construction and administration of USS preserved-benefit rules.
enrichment.outcome: Declaration granted that actuarial reduction must not be applied where preserved benefits are paid on or after a member's contractual retirement date; OPB correspondence did not sanction the trustee's practice.
enrichment.ratio: Normal pension age under section 180(1)(b) of the Pension Schemes Act 1993 must be determined by reference to the particular member's terms of employment, so short-service preserved benefits cannot be actuarially reduced when brought into payment at the contractual retirement age if long-service benefits at that age would not be reduced.
legal_issues: Whether normal pension age is a scheme-wide or member-specific concept under section 180
Whether rule 9.5(d) permitted actuarial reduction of preserved benefits taken at contractual retirement age
Whether the Occupational Pensions Board had determined or modified the preservation requirements to permit the trustee's practice
How cash equivalent transfer values should be calculated

notes: Prison adjudication Ezeh follow-on; victim status and adequacy of remitting added days are clearly decided.

enrichment.short_title: Prison adjudication after Ezeh: whether guilt finding must be quashed
key_facts: Serving prisoner Napier was found guilty at a governor's adjudication of assaulting an officer by throwing excrement and urine and received 35 added days.
After Ezeh and Connors v United Kingdom, the Secretary of State remitted added days imposed after 2 October 2000 but refused to quash the finding of guilt.
Napier sought judicial review, arguing he remained a victim because the Article 6 breach left a culpability finding on his record affecting CSC management.
The challenge did not seek to quash his Closed Supervision Centre allocation itself.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application for judicial review of the Secretary of State's refusal to quash a prison adjudication finding after remitting the penalty.
enrichment.outcome: Application refused; remission of added days was adequate redress and the claimant was no longer a victim under Article 34.
enrichment.ratio: Ezeh turned on the punitive deprivation of liberty from added days; once that penalty was remitted, the adjudication did not have to comply with Article 6 and the governor's finding could stand as an administrative finding of fact for prison management without requiring quashing.
legal_issues: The effect of Ezeh where added days had been remitted but the finding of guilt remained
Whether the claimant remained a victim entitled to a remedy under Article 34
Whether adequate redress required quashing the factual finding as well as remitting punishment
Whether potential added days alone made the adjudication a criminal charge under the Engel criteria

notes: First Attorney General reference on human trafficking; sentencing uplift to 23 years and guidance are clearly set out.

enrichment.short_title: Attorney General reference: 23-year sentence for trafficking young girls into prostitution
key_facts: An Albanian-born offender trafficked seven young women into the UK and coerced several into prostitution over about three years.
He pleaded guilty to assisting unlawful immigration and was convicted after trial of living on immoral earnings, kidnapping and incitement to rape.
The Crown Court imposed a total sentence of 10 years, including 10-year kidnapping terms treated as concurrent anchors.
Police traced over £204,000 through his bank accounts and found prostitution paraphernalia at his London address.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Attorney General's reference for leave to refer unduly lenient sentences on human trafficking and related offences.
enrichment.outcome: Leave granted; total sentence increased from 10 to 23 years with consecutive terms structured by victim-related counts.
enrichment.ratio: Human trafficking involving coercion, kidnapping and sexual exploitation demands lengthy deterrent sentences well above previous tariffs; assisting unlawful immigration in a commercial exploitation context warrants five years per count and living on immoral earnings with coercion warrants up to five years.
legal_issues: Appropriate sentencing levels for human trafficking and sexual exploitation of trafficked victims
Whether concurrent structuring adequately reflected overall criminality
Sentencing for assisting unlawful immigration where the maximum had increased to 10 years
Tariffs for kidnapping, living on immoral earnings and incitement to rape in trafficking cases

notes: Murder appeal turning on Vye good character direction; new evidence refused and conviction quashed for direction error.

enrichment.short_title: Murder appeal: defective good character direction for 18-year-old defendant

statutes_considered.title: Criminal Justice and Public Order Act 1994

key_facts: John Gray, aged 18, was convicted of murder after a fracas at an employment agency in which the victim was stabbed upstairs.
The critical issue was whether Gray went upstairs with his father and co-defendant or remained outside as he claimed.
Gray had one minor driving offence and admitted some violence on the ground floor but received no full Vye good character direction.
Proposed new evidence from a passer-by and from a witness about the father discarding a knife was rejected as incapable of affecting the verdict.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against conviction by leave of the single judge on good character and section 34 directions, with applications to add fresh evidence.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed and conviction quashed for material irregularity in the good character direction; fresh evidence applications refused.
enrichment.ratio: Where a defendant with a minor unrelated conviction should be treated as of effective good character, the trial judge must give a full modified Vye direction on both credibility and propensity; a grudging credibility-only direction after refusing to treat the defendant as of good character is a material irregularity in a case turning on the defendant's account against an eyewitness.
legal_issues: Whether the judge should have treated Gray as a defendant of effective good character
Whether a full two-limb Vye direction was required despite admitted violence at the scene
Whether the section 34 direction adequately reminded the jury of circumstances existing at interview
Whether new witness evidence should be admitted on appeal

notes: SEN school placement statutory appeal; Tribunal discretion and section 9 cost balancing reviewed without error found.

enrichment.short_title: Special educational needs appeal: Christ's School preferred over independent placement
key_facts: A 13-year-old boy with achromatopsia had been privately funded at St James's School for two years with specialist visual equipment.
Richmond LEA proposed naming maintained Christ's School in his statement of special educational needs as an appropriate and cheaper placement.
The Special Educational Needs Tribunal found Christ's could meet his needs with transitional support and escorted travel arrangements.
Parents argued the Tribunal applied an adequacy rather than appropriateness test and failed to weigh safety, curriculum and cost factors.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Statutory appeal under section 11 of the Tribunals and Inquiries Act 1992 against a SEND Tribunal decision on Part 4 school placement.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; no error of law identified in the Tribunal's decision to specify Christ's School.
enrichment.ratio: On appeal the court reviews legal error only; where a Tribunal expressly finds a maintained school appropriate to meet a visually impaired pupil's needs and balances parental preference against reasonable public expenditure under section 9, it is not unlawful to prefer the cheaper maintained placement if safety and support concerns have been addressed.
legal_issues: Whether the Tribunal applied an adequacy test rather than the statutory appropriateness test
Whether safety, travel and curriculum factors were ignored or misweighted
Whether the Tribunal erred in its cost comparison between St James's and Christ's School
Whether the Tribunal should have named a type of school including independent schools rather than a specific maintained school

notes: Police injury pension medical referee decision; treatment assumption under Regulation A12(1A) inadequately reasoned and quashed.

enrichment.short_title: Police injury pension appeal: medical referee erred on anxiety permanency
key_facts: Former West Yorkshire officer Bostock retired on ill-health grounds with chronic anxiety linked by most medical evidence to traumatic police incidents.
Force medical officer Dr Shinn certified anxiety as injury on duty but not likely permanent; hypertension was excluded from challenge.
Medical referee dismissed the appeal, doubting work causation and finding permanency not established partly because Bostock received no treatment.
Consultant evidence described return to frontline duties as incompatible with Bostock's psychological state.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application for judicial review of a medical referee's decision on appeal under the Police Pensions Regulations 1987.
enrichment.outcome: Ground 2 on asking the wrong permanency question failed; ground 1 succeeded and the determination was quashed and remitted to a fresh medical referee.
enrichment.ratio: Under Regulation A12(1A), assuming appropriate medical treatment does not mean disablement is non-permanent simply because the officer is not currently receiving treatment; the referee must consider whether treatment would realistically eliminate disablement from ordinary police duties in a work-linked anxiety case.
legal_issues: Whether the medical referee asked the correct permanency question under Regulation A12
How Regulation A12(1A) on assumed appropriate medical treatment should be applied
Whether sparse reasoning rendered the treatment analysis unlawful
Whether disablement from police duties rather than permanence of the illness was the focus of the inquiry

notes: CPR disclosure dispute in bank security case; paragraph 2 specific disclosure order varied on appeal as disproportionate.

enrichment.short_title: Punjab National Bank security claim: appeal on lost-document disclosure order
key_facts: The bank claimed circa 1980s security over £2 million properties allegedly securing a company debt, while defendants alleged an oral 1986 compromise.
Initial disclosure was minimal and further documents emerged only after cross-examination of the former London branch manager.
Schedule C listed lost or destroyed documents in blanket terms without itemising individual documents.
The deputy judge ordered inspection of enforcement files and a wide list of missing documents referred to in disclosed papers.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Renewed application for permission to appeal against disclosure and inspection orders, refusal of mediation, and costs in an adjourned trial.
enrichment.outcome: Permission refused on inspection of enforcement files and mediation; permission granted on paragraph 2 and appeal allowed to replace that order with a narrower London-documents exercise based on the defendant's list.
enrichment.ratio: Where a party gives only blanket statements of lost or destroyed documents in exceptional circumstances the court may require itemisation, but an order forcing review of all files to identify every referenced missing document may be disproportionate; a refined list-based process focused on readily accessible documents is preferable before any further inspection in India.
legal_issues: Whether CPR 31.10 required itemisation of each lost or destroyed document
Whether the judge could order inspection of undisclosed enforcement files under rule 31.12
Whether paragraph 2 of the disclosure order was disproportionate
Whether the judge erred in refusing a mediation order

notes: Youth Court committal for trial challenge; Southampton principles applied and both 14-year-olds' committals quashed.

enrichment.short_title: Youth Court committal quashed for 14-year-olds charged with mobile phone robbery
key_facts: Two 14-year-olds of previous good character were committed to the Crown Court for trial for robbery of a mobile phone and sovereign ring by a group of up to 15 youths.
W admitted striking the victim with a crutch; M denied involvement beyond presence at the scene.
Because neither was a persistent offender, the Youth Court could not impose a detention and training order and a non-custodial sentence would follow on conviction.
The district judge committed on grounds of group size, violence and mobile phone robbery prevalence.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Applications for judicial review of Youth Court decisions to decline jurisdiction and commit for trial under section 24.
enrichment.outcome: Permission granted to W and consolidated with M; committal decisions quashed for both claimants.
enrichment.ratio: A Youth Court should commit a non-persistent offender under 15 only if there is a real prospect of a section 91 custodial sentence of or approaching two years; the mere unavailability of a detention and training order is not an exceptional circumstance justifying committal, and group robbery by young first offenders did not meet that threshold here.
legal_issues: The test for declining jurisdiction under section 24 and section 91(3)
Whether there was a real possibility of a two-year custodial sentence for 14-year-olds of good character
The effect of section 100(2) limiting detention and training orders for under-15 non-persistent offenders
Whether Attorney General robbery sentencing guidance applied equally to very young offenders
